content: Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim injection is a sulfonamide antibiotic combination approved by the FDA for treating specific bacterial infections, including urinary tract infections (UTIs), acute otitis media in pediatric patients, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, shigellosis, Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia (PJP), prophylaxis against PJP, and traveler’s diarrhea. It is essential to use this medication only for infections caused by bacteria proven or strongly suspected to be susceptible to the drug. For adults, the typical dosage for treating UTIs is one double-strength Bactrim tablet or two regular-strength tablets every 12 hours for 10 to 14 days. For shigellosis, the same dosage is used for five days. In cases of acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, the dosage is one double-strength tablet or two regular-strength tablets every 12 hours for 14 days. For traveler’s diarrhea, the recommended dosage is the same but for five days. Dosage adjustments are necessary for patients with impaired renal function. In pediatric patients, Bactrim is contraindicated for those under two months of age. For children with UTIs or acute otitis media, the recommended dose is 40 mg/kg of sulfamethoxazole and 8 mg/kg of trimethoprim per 24 hours, divided into two doses every 12 hours for 10 days. For shigellosis, the same dosage is used for five days. Prophylactic dosing for children involves 750 mg/m²/day of sulfamethoxazole and 150 mg/m²/day of trimethoprim, divided into two doses on three consecutive days per week. Bactrim is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to sulfonamides or trimethoprim, a history of drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia, or documented megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency. It is also contraindicated in pediatric patients under two months of age, those with severe renal insufficiency when renal function cannot be monitored, and those with marked hepatic damage. Warnings include the potential for severe adverse reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, fulminant hepatic necrosis, agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, and other blood dyscrasias. Fatalities have been reported in rare cases. Sulfonamides should be discontinued at the first sign of skin rash or other adverse reactions. Hypersensitivity reactions, including pulmonary infiltrates, have been reported. Immune-mediated thrombocytopenia can occur and may be life-threatening. Sulfonamides are not effective for eradicating group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infections and should not be used for this purpose. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including Bactrim, and may range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. If CDAD is suspected, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. During pregnancy, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim should only be used if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus, as it may interfere with folic acid metabolism. Some epidemiologic studies suggest an association between first-trimester exposure and an increased risk of congenital malformations, such as neural tube defects and cardiovascular abnormalities. However, other studies have not found statistically significant associations. In nursing mothers, caution is advised as the drug is excreted in breast milk. It should be avoided in breastfeeding jaundiced, ill, stressed, or premature infants due to the risk of bilirubin displacement and kernicterus. Elderly patients may experience more severe adverse reactions, including skin reactions, bone marrow suppression, and hyperkalemia. Dosage adjustments are recommended for those with impaired renal function, and the duration of use should be minimized to reduce the risk of adverse effects. Drug interactions include the potential for sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim to inhibit CYP2C9, CYP2C8, and OCT2 enzymes, leading to interactions with drugs metabolized by these pathways. Caution is advised when co-administering Bactrim with warfarin, phenytoin, methotrexate, cyclosporine, digoxin, and other drugs. Monitoring of serum levels and clinical effects is recommended in such cases. Adverse reactions commonly include gastrointestinal disturbances (nausea, vomiting, anorexia) and allergic skin reactions (rash, urticaria). Rare but severe reactions include Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, and fulminant hepatic necrosis. Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia have also been reported, particularly in patients with underlying conditions or those receiving high doses. Patients receiving Bactrim should maintain adequate fluid intake to prevent crystalluria. Regular monitoring of blood counts, renal function, and serum potassium is recommended during therapy, especially in patients with predisposing conditions.
